meta.task: M1-19 / M5 — sourced dog data for realism
meta.status: Imported into breed_stage_params (M5-R01, BreedStageParamsSeeder). Game values David confirmed on 2026-10-05 carry a "decision" field. M5-R03 (2026-10-06): training values added (learning multiplier, individual variation — David decisions; minutes, progress, decay, effects — proposals). M5-R03b (2026-10-06): David confirmed minutes, progress and decay; starting progress per arrival stage added (decision); the two effects stay proposals.

conventions.confidence: high = breed standard / peer-reviewed / vet association and consistent across sources; medium = single reputable source or sources disagree a little; low = secondary source, strong disagreement, or derived/proposal
conventions.unsourced: Anything with source_id null is marked 'UNSOURCED — proposal' and must not be shown to parents/children as fact.
conventions.quotes: Quotes are as returned by the web-fetch tool on 2026-10-05; spot-check against the URL before import.
conventions.game_time: 1 real week = 1 month of dog age (REALISM_SPEC §2).
conventions.decision: "potrdil David 2026-10-05: …" = the game value David confirmed (DECISIONS 2026-10-05). It is a product decision, NOT literature: source_id stays the underlying evidence and is null where the literature gives no number.

salt_2017_bands_kg.quote: Category I: <6.5 kg … Category IV: 15 to <30 kg; Category V: 30 to <40 kg
salt_2017_bands_kg.notes: Category IV breeds: Australian Shepherd, Chow Chow, Basset Hound, Siberian Husky, English Bulldog, Pit Bull type, Boxer. Border Collie not listed.

puppy.quote: From birth to cessation of rapid growth (~6–9 months, varying with breed and size)

young_adult.quote: From cessation of rapid growth to completion of physical and social maturation, which occurs in most dogs by 3 to 4 years of age
young_adult.notes: AAHA has no separate 'adolescent' stage; it is inside 'young adult'.
young_adult.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: young stage starts at 9 months (upper end of ~6–9 months)

adolescence.quote: dog adolescence (which typically begins between six to nine months of age) … during puberty (at around eight months of age)
adolescence.notes: Press summary of Asher & Harvey, Biology Letters 2020 (guide-dog puppies, n=285). End of adolescence not stated.

mature_adult.value: 3–4 years → start of last 25% of lifespan
mature_adult.quote: From completion of physical and social maturation until the last 25% of estimated lifespan (breed and size dependent)
mature_adult.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: adult stage starts at 36 months (lower end of 3–4 years)

senior.quote: From the last 25% of estimated lifespan through end-of-life.

senior_rule_of_thumb.quote: Dogs over the age of seven can be considered 'senior' … dogs aged over 12 can be considered 'geriatric.'
senior_rule_of_thumb.notes: UK charity rule of thumb, not size-specific; conflicts with AAHA 25% rule for long-lived dogs.

adult_weight_reached_by_size.quote: very small dogs reaching maturity at between 8 and 12 months of age and larger breeds requiring up to 24 months to reach adult body weight

growth_end_by_size_class.notes: Growth stops when growth plates seal (S10); no plate-closure ages given.

growth_plate_closure.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. No veterinary source with plate-closure ages per size was found; use 'growth_end_by_size_class' instead.

logistic_model.description: Logistic curve y = a / (1 + exp(-(x - x0)/b)), x in weeks. Shape parameters = arithmetic mean of the four 'medium' breeds in S9 (Fox Terrier, Teckel, Basset Hound, Beagle); a = adult weight of the target dog.
logistic_model.check: Implied time to 99 percent adult weight = x0 + b*ln(99) = 57.4 weeks, consistent with S9 T99 of 52-58 weeks for the medium breeds.
logistic_model.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. Neither Border Collie nor mixed breeds were in S9 (21 dogs). Applying the medium-breed shape to them is an assumption. Interpretation of 1/b as % per week is ours; it is consistent with the reported T99. Model is not valid near birth.

percent_of_adult_weight_by_month.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. Computed from logistic_model (S9 medium-breed shape).

8_12_weeks.quote: Puppies eight to 12 weeks old need four meals a day.
8_12_weeks.notes: RKC (S21): 'From two to three months – four meals a day'. RSPCA AU (S20): 'at least 4 times per day to begin with'.

3_6_months.quote: Feed puppies three to six months old three meals a day.
3_6_months.notes: RKC (S21): 'From four to six months – two to three meals a day'.

6_12_months.quote: Feed puppies six months to one year two meals a day.
6_12_months.notes: RKC (S21): 'Over six months – two meals a day (depending on the breed)'.

adult.quote: The most common recommendation is to feed your dog at least two meals per day.
adult.notes: Sources disagree: ASPCA (S18) 'one meal a day is usually enough' after the first birthday; RSPCA AU (S20) 'adult dogs should be fed at least twice per day to help avoid bloat'. 2 chosen as majority.

senior.quote: feeding your dog smaller meals two or three times a day
senior.notes: AAHA (S13): 'Maintenance energy requirements (MER) generally decrease over a dog's lifetime.'
senior.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: senior = 2 meals/day (lower end of 2–3)

hunger_physiology.unit: hours after a meal until hunger signals
hunger_physiology.quote: After 8 to 10 hours, an empty stomach begins to send signals to the brain that stimulate a hunger response.
hunger_physiology.notes: Useful for hunger decay calibration of adults.

daily_requirement.quote: Generally, dogs require 60-80 ml of water per kg of body weight
daily_requirement.notes: FirstVet (S23): normal 'between 20-70ml/kg body weight per day'; abnormal 'more than 100ml/kg'. Sources differ; general only, not by age or breed.

excessive_threshold.quote: more than 100ml/kg body weight per day

availability.quote: Clean, fresh water should be available at all times
availability.notes: RSPCA AU (S20): 'Fresh drinking water must be available at all times'. No source gives a number of refills per day.

refills_per_day.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. Game abstraction only (current breed_configs value). Real advice is 'water always available'; no source supports a refill count.

puppy_rule_of_thumb.value: 5 min × age in months, twice a day, until full-grown
puppy_rule_of_thumb.quote: five minutes of exercise per month of age, twice a day, until the puppy is full-grown
puppy_rule_of_thumb.notes: CONTESTED: Veterinary Ireland Journal (S25) lists it among 'misconceptions like five minutes of exercise per month of life'. No study behind the number was found.
puppy_rule_of_thumb.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: puppy and young dog = 10 min/day × age in months, capped at the adult minutes (rule stays contested, confidence low)

puppy_evidence.value: off-lead exercise on soft ground ≤ 3 months protective; stairs ≤ 3 months risk
puppy_evidence.quote: puppies ≤ 3 months old should not be allowed access to stairs, but should be allowed outdoor exercise on soft ground
puppy_evidence.notes: Only Newfoundland, Labrador, Leonberger, Irish Wolfhound (large/giant).

adult_general.quote: all adult dogs should receive between 30 minutes and two hours of physical activity and mental stimulation daily

senior.value: frequent short walks instead of one long one
senior.quote: try to go for frequent short walks instead of one long one

steps_conversion.unit: human steps per minute of walking
steps_conversion.quote: ≥100 steps/min is a consistent heuristic … associated with absolutely defined moderate intensity (3 metabolic equivalents (METs))
steps_conversion.notes: ASSUMPTION for the game: child's steps = walk minutes × 100. S45 covers ADULTS only ('cadence-based research in children and adolescents is currently less developed'). No veterinary source gives a step goal for dogs (see S46).

measured_16_weeks.quote: mean total hours of sleep in this subpopulation was reported as 11.2 h (SD = 2.9)
measured_16_weeks.notes: Owner-reported cohort (Dogs Trust Generation Pup). Lower than RKC figures — conflict; RKC may include dozing/resting.

senior.value: sleep more; daytime sleep + night restlessness is a sign of cognitive dysfunction
senior.quote: can become less energetic and tend to sleep more
senior.notes: AAHA (S13): 'daytime sleeping and nighttime restlessness' are the most common clinical signs of cognitive dysfunction (DISHAA). No hours given.

hold_bladder.value: 1 hour per month of age (±1 h)
hold_bladder.quote: one hour for each month of age, give or take an hour
hold_bladder.notes: WebMD/DVM-reviewed (S31): '1 hour for every month of age until they're about a year old'.

adult_hold.quote: can reasonably be expected to hold their urine for 8 hours or longer … about every four hours when possible

when_to_go_out.value: after eating, naps, strenuous play, change of activity
when_to_go_out.quote: puppies may need to eliminate after eating, naps, strenuous play, or whenever there is a change of activity

consistent_from.quote: they may not become consistent until they're between 12 and 16 weeks old

fully_trained.quote: It typically takes 4-6 months for a puppy to be fully house trained, but some puppies may take up to a year.

accidents.quote: Accidents are common with puppies up to a year old.
accidents.notes: No accident frequency (per day) found in any source.

daytime_trips_puppy.quote: you can expect to take puppies out every 2 hours or so during the day

learns_to_signal.value: a house-trained puppy can learn to 'ask' to go out (door, bell)
learns_to_signal.quote: Once your puppy is physically mature enough to hold her bladder consistently, she can learn to 'ask' to be taken outside.
learns_to_signal.notes: VCA (S47, E. Lindell VMD DACVB): 'She may develop a signal on her own, such as coming to you and barking, or going to the door and scratching.' Basis of the game effect potty training → fewer accidents (M5-R03); the size of the effect is not sourced.

baby_teeth_in.quote: By now all of your puppy's baby teeth should have come in. Dogs usually have about 28 baby teeth total

baby_teeth_shed.quote: your puppy's baby teeth start to shed (Weeks 12-16)

adult_teeth_in.quote: By the time, your puppy is about six months old or so, all of their puppy teeth should have fallen out, and their adult teeth should have grown in.

intense_chewing_ends.quote: This intensified chewing phase usually ends by six months of age.

destructive_chewing_causes.quote: Bored dogs tend look for ways to entertain themselves, and chewing is one option.

exercise_vs_boredom.value: daily exercise and mental stimulation reduce boredom-driven behaviour
exercise_vs_boredom.quote: Daily exercise and mental stimulation may diminish tendency to seek novelty from boredom

guidance_reduces_chewing.value: guidance / training restricts chewing to appropriate objects
guidance_reduces_chewing.quote: Although puppies do need to chew on things, gentle guidance can teach your puppy to restrict chewing to appropriate objects, like his own toys.
guidance_reduces_chewing.notes: ASPCA (S33), fetched 2026-10-06. Basis of the game effect 'place' training → less chewing (M5-R03); the size of the effect is not sourced.

start_age.quote: Puppies can begin very simple training starting as soon as they come home, usually around 8 weeks old.
start_age.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: a puppy arrives at 2 months

session_length_puppy.quote: Always keep training sessions brief — just five to 10 minutes
session_length_puppy.notes: PetMD (S37): 'about five minutes each … no more than 15 minutes per day'.

daily_total_puppy.quote: try to average a total of no more than 15 minutes per day

first_commands.quote: Teach Your Dog to Come When Called, Loose-Leash Walking, Sit, Down, Stay

socialization_window.quote: socialization must happen during the sensitive period (~3 to 14 weeks of age)

adolescent_obedience_dip.quote: a reduction in obedience, during puberty (at around eight months of age)

adult_session_length.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. No source found for adult session length.

coren_tiers.unit: repetitions to learn a new command / % obeys first command
coren_tiers.quote: Brightest Dogs Understanding of new commands: fewer than 5 repetitions.; Obey first command: 95% of the time or better.
coren_tiers.notes: Secondary source (Wikipedia). Survey of obedience judges, not an experiment; verify in the book before use.

all_dogs_median_uk.quote: On average, companion dogs live for 12.5 years.

medium_breeds_median_uk.quote: medium-sized breeds were found to live longer, with lifespans of 12.5 years

size_effect.quote: increasing bodyweight was negatively correlated with longevity

identity.value: FCI No. 297, Group 1 Section 1, Great Britain
identity.quote: Standard Number: 297; Group 1 - Shepherd and Cattle Dogs; Country of Origin: Great Britain

fci_ideal.quote: Ideal height at withers: Males: 53 cm (21 ins), Females: slightly less.

akc_range.quote: The height at the withers varies from 19 to 22 inches for males, 18 to 21 inches for females.

akc.notes: Neither FCI nor AKC standard gives weight.

pdsa.notes: Conflicts with AKC; heavier than Salt category IV typical. Prefer AKC.

salt_category.value: IV (15–<30 kg) — by AKC weight it spans III/IV
salt_category.notes: Border Collie itself was not in the Salt dataset; category assignment by weight is ours.

weight_by_month_kg.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. = AKC adult range × logistic % (general_by_size.growth.logistic_model).

senior_from.notes: Derived: AAHA senior = last 25% of lifespan (S11) × median 13.1 y (S15) → 0.75 × 13.1 = 9.8 y. Dogs Trust rule of thumb says > 7 y (S14).
senior_from.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: senior from 118 months (0.75 × 13.1 y)

adult.quote: Exercise: More than 2 hours per day
adult.notes: PDSA (S7): 'a minimum of two hours exercise every day'.

temperament.value: tenacious, hard-working, great tractability; keen, alert, responsive, intelligent; neither nervous nor aggressive
temperament.quote: Tenacious, hard-working, of great tractability. Keen, alert, responsive and intelligent. Neither nervous nor aggressive.

boredom_chewing.quote: If left alone or not given enough exercise, your Collie will certainly let you know they're unhappy by chewing anything in paw's reach!

herding_children.quote: natural herding instincts may lead them to herd children during play

mental_stimulation.quote: always need to have something to do, so making sure they have mental stimulation is very important

coren_rank.quote: 190 of the 199 judges ranked the Border Collie in the top 10
coren_rank.notes: Rank 1 of 130+ breeds (S35). Coren: measures 'working and obedience intelligence' only.

coren_tier.quote: Brightest Dogs … fewer than 5 repetitions … 95% of the time or better
coren_tier.notes: Tier definitions from Wikipedia; verify in book.

genetic_biddability.value: Border Collie ancestry associated with higher biddability
genetic_biddability.quote: border collie ancestry correlates with increased biddability
genetic_biddability.notes: But breed explains ~9% of individual behaviour variation (S42) — individual dogs vary.

learning_multiplier.notes: UNSOURCED as a number — game value. Coren ranks the Border Collie #1 (S34) and puts it in the 'brightest' tier (<5 repetitions to learn a command vs 25–40 for 'average', S35 — secondary source), but gives no speed factor. Training progress per correctly timed praise × 2.
learning_multiplier.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-06: Border Collie learns ~2× faster than the mixed-breed baseline (M5-R03)

general.value: well proportioned, smooth outline, sufficient substance for endurance
general.quote: Well proportioned, smooth outline showing quality, gracefulness and perfect balance, combined with sufficient substance to give impression of endurance.

coat_varieties.quote: Two varieties: Moderately long or Smooth. In both, topcoat dense and medium textured, undercoat soft and dense
coat_varieties.notes: AKC (S3) also two varieties, double coat.

colour_rule.value: any colour; white must never predominate (FCI/UK); AKC: all colours/combinations equal
colour_rule.quote: Variety of colours permissible. White should never predominate.
colour_rule.notes: AKC (S3): 'appears in all colors or combination of colors and/or markings. All colors are to be judged equally'. No standard lists specific colours or their frequencies.

colour_list_and_weights.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. Specific colour names (black & white, tricolour, red, blue, merles, sable) and their frequencies are NOT in FCI/AKC/UK standards. The AKC breed page colour list could not be accessed. Draft weights in breed_appearance.php are unsourced.

ears.quote: Carried erect or semi-erect and sensitive in use.
ears.notes: AKC (S3): 'one or both carried erect and/or semi-erect' → supports mixed carriage.

eyes.value: brown; in merles one or both, or part of one or both, may be blue
eyes.quote: Brown in colour except in merles where one or both or part of one or both may be blue.
eyes.notes: RKC (S6) identical. AKC (S3): 'Any eye color is acceptable, but blue eyes in dogs other than merle are not preferred.' Amber is not named by any standard.

tail.value: moderately long, low set, upward swirl towards end
tail.quote: Moderately long, the bone reaching at least to hock, set on low, well-furnished and with an upward swirl towards the end.

face_markings.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. No standard describes blaze / face markings. Draft 'markings' list is unsourced.

labrador_retriever._note: Added 2026-10-09 (M5-R10-01). Quotes as returned by the web-fetch tool on 2026-10-09; spot-check before import (sources.md S48–S62).

identity.value: FCI No. 122, Group 8 Section 1 (Retrievers), Great Britain
identity.quote: Standard number: 122; Group n°8 - Chiens rapporteurs de gibier - Chiens leveurs de gibier - Chiens d'eau; Section: Rapporteurs de gibier; Country of origin: GRANDE-BRETAGNE
identity.notes: FCI standard (S48): 'Group 8 Retrievers, Flushing dogs, Water dogs. Section 1 Retrievers.' 'UTILIZATION: Retriever.' Definitive FCI acceptance 24/12/1954 (S49). NOTE: both S48 and S49 give 'DATE OF PUBLICATION OF THE OFFICIAL VALID STANDARD: 08.09.2026' (EN version dated 06.10.2026) — a very recent revision; verify on fci.be.

size_class.notes: PDSA (S53): 'Size: Large'. Woodgreen (S60): 'Size: Large'. AKC breed page (S62) calls it a 'medium-to-large dog'.

fci_ideal.quote: Ideal height at the withers: Males: 56 – 57 cm. Females: 54 – 56 cm.
fci_ideal.notes: RKC standard (S51) differs for bitches: 'Ideal height at withers: dogs: 56-57 cms (22-22½ ins); bitches: 55-56 cms (21½-22 ins).' PDSA (S53): 'Height: 55-57 cm'.

rkc_ideal.quote: Ideal height at withers: dogs: 56-57 cms (22-22½ ins); bitches: 55-56 cms (21½-22 ins).
rkc_ideal.notes: Bitch lower limit 55 cm vs FCI 54 cm (S48).

akc_range.quote: The height at the withers for a dog is 22½ to 24½ inches; for a bitch is 21½ to 23½ inches.
akc_range.notes: AKC allows taller dogs than FCI/RKC (up to 62.2 cm vs 57 cm).

akc.unit: kg (converted from dogs 65–80 lb, bitches 55–70 lb)
akc.quote: Approximate weight of dogs and bitches in working condition: dogs 65 to 80 pounds; bitches 55 to 70 pounds.
akc.notes: From the AKC breed standard (approved 1994). Overall 24.9–36.3 kg. FCI (S48) and RKC (S51) standards give no weight.

uk_measured_mean.quote: The mean adult bodyweight of males (35.2 kg, SD 5.9 kg) was higher than for females (30.4 kg, SD 5.2 kg) (P < 0.001).
uk_measured_mean.notes: Measured in UK primary-care Labradors (VetCompass, McGreevy et al. 2018). Males average at the top of the AKC range; note 8.8 % were recorded overweight/obese.

salt_category.value: V (30–<40 kg) by measured UK means; AKC range spans IV/V
salt_category.quote: Category IV: 15 to <30 kg; Category V: 30 to <40 kg
salt_category.notes: Category assignment by weight is ours; whether Salt 2017 listed the Labrador in a category could not be checked (PMC not reachable 2026-10-09).

adult_weight_reached.notes: Size-class value, not breed-specific. Labrador AKC males 65–80 lb are 'Large'; bitches 55–70 lb straddle Medium (24–59 lb: 12–15 months) and Large. Salt (S8): 'larger breeds requiring up to 24 months to reach adult body weight'. Quote is a table row on the page (Large (59–99 pounds) | 15–18 months).

weight_by_month_kg.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. Not derived: the existing logistic shape (general_by_size.growth.logistic_model) is a MEDIUM-breed curve (≈99 % at 57 weeks) and would contradict the large-breed 15–18 months (S10). A large-breed curve needs a source (S9 has no large breed; Salt 2017 raw data not downloadable). Open question for David.

median_uk.notes: McMillan et al. 2024 (Sci Rep), corrected Figure 3 legend (author correction, same document as S16, read from the LJMU repository copy because PMC was not reachable). The Dogs Trust summary page (S15) does not list the Labrador. Conflicts with S55 (12.0 y).

median_uk_vetcompass_2018.quote: The median longevity of Labrador retrievers overall was 12.0 years (IQR 9.9–13.8, range 0.0–16.0).
median_uk_vetcompass_2018.notes: McGreevy, Wilson, …, O'Neill (2018) — VetCompass, 33,320 Labradors under care in 2013; longevity from the deaths in a random sample. Colour effect: 'The median longevity of non-chocolate coloured dogs (n = 139, 12.1 years…' vs '…chocolate coloured animals (n = 34, 10.7 years…' (S55; press summary S56).

senior_from.notes: Derived: AAHA senior = last 25% of lifespan (S11) × median 13.1 y (S54) → 0.75 × 13.1 = 9.8 y = 118 months (same as Border Collie). With the VetCompass median 12.0 y (S55): 0.75 × 12.0 = 9.0 y = 108 months. Dogs Trust rule of thumb > 7 y (S14).

adult.quote: Exercise: More than 2 hours per day
adult.notes: Sources disagree: Guide Dogs UK (S59): 'Labrador retrievers generally need at least 90 minutes of exercise daily as adults.'; Woodgreen (S60): 'Exercise needs: 60-90 mins'; PDSA (S53) gives no minutes: 'Full of energy, Labradors need a lot of exercise and mental enrichment each day to keep them physically fit'. Confidence lowered to medium for the conflict.

energy.quote: Full of energy, Labradors need a lot of exercise and mental enrichment each day to keep them physically fit

temperament.value: good-tempered, very agile; intelligent, keen and biddable, strong will to please; kindly, no aggression or undue shyness; adaptable, devoted companion
temperament.quote: Good-tempered, very agile. Excellent nose, soft mouth; keen lover of water. Adaptable, devoted companion. Intelligent, keen and biddable, with a strong will to please. Kindly nature, with no trace of aggression or undue shyness.
temperament.notes: Returned by the tool in three consecutive fragments; RKC (S51) same wording ('keen love of water'). AKC (S52): 'The ideal disposition is one of a kindly, outgoing, tractable nature;' 'eager to please and non-aggressive towards man or animal.'

food_motivation.quote: They're generally described as intelligent, enjoy learning, and highly food motivated
food_motivation.notes: Cambridge (S58): 'People who live with Labradors often say they are obsessed by food.' S55: 'They are often of stocky build with a tendency to eat beyond their physiological needs...'. Genetic basis: S57.

pomc_deletion.value: POMC gene deletion associated with higher body weight and greater food motivation; ~23 % of Labradors carry ≥1 copy
pomc_deletion.quote: The deletion … associated with body weight (per allele effect of 0.33 SD) … greater food motivation; allele frequency of 12%
pomc_deletion.notes: Raffan et al. 2016, Cell Metab 23:893–900 (abstract fragments as returned; ellipses ours). Press release (S58): 'Around one in four (23%) Labradors is thought to carry at least one copy of the variant.' and 'for each copy of the gene carried, the dog was on average 1.9kg heavier.'

obesity_tendency.value: prone to obesity; 8.8 % recorded overweight/obese in UK primary care
obesity_tendency.notes: S55: 'overweight/obesity (183, 8.8%, 95% CI: 7.6–10.1)' — 2nd most common disorder after otitis externa (10.4 %). S56: 'We found that 8.8 percent of UK Labradors are overweight or obese.'

chewing.value: retrievers chew a lot through adolescence (to ~2 years)
chewing.quote: Retrievers, especially, are known for their love of chewing throughout their adolescence
chewing.notes: Single tier-C source (vet column, 2012); the saying 'Chew till they're two; shed till they're dead.' is folklore, not data. Same page attributes it to the retrieving instinct and too little exercise. No tier A/B Labrador-specific chewing source found.

family.value: bonds with the whole family; good family pet with socialisation
family.quote: They usually bond well with the whole family and are affectionate and loving.
family.notes: PDSA (S53): 'Labradors make perfect family pets, given the right socialisation, as with all breeds.'

coren_rank.notes: Rank 7 in Coren's list as reproduced on Wikipedia (table row). Coren's own article (S34) could not be fetched on 2026-10-09 — verify in the book. Top 10: Border Collie, Poodle, German Shepherd, Golden Retriever, Doberman, Shetland Sheepdog, Labrador, Papillon, Rottweiler, Australian Cattle Dog.

coren_tier.quote: Understanding of new commands: fewer than 5 repetitions.; Obey first command: 95% of the time or better.;
coren_tier.notes: Same tier as the Border Collie (ranks 1–10). Tier definitions from Wikipedia; verify in book.

training_notes.value: obedient, quick to learn, eager to please; treats work well
training_notes.quote: They're obedient, quick to learn and eager to please.
training_notes.notes: Guide Dogs UK (S59): 'With their known famed love of food, Labradors may enjoy treats as part of training and food-based games and puzzles.' Woodgreen (S60): 'Training: Moderately easy'.

general.value: strongly built, short-coupled, very active; broad skull; broad, deep chest
general.quote: Strongly built, short-coupled, very active; broad in skull; broad and deep through chest and ribs; broad and strong over loins and hindquarters.
general.notes: RKC (S51) adds that agility 'precludes excessive body weight or excessive substance'.

colours.quote: Wholly black, yellow or liver/chocolate. Yellows range from light cream to fox red, livers/chocolates range from light to dark.
colours.notes: Solid colours only: 'Small white spot on chest and the rear of pasterns permissible.' 'Any other colour or combination of colours unacceptable.' RKC (S51): 'The only correct colours are wholly black, yellow and liver/chocolate.' AKC (S52): 'The Labrador Retriever coat colors are black, yellow and chocolate.' Colour frequencies: not sourced.

colour_weights.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. No source gives colour frequencies. Note for game: chocolate Labradors had a shorter median life (10.7 vs 12.1 y, S55) — do not model unless David wants it.

coat.value: short, dense, no wave or feathering, fairly hard to the touch; weather-resistant undercoat
coat.quote: Distinctive feature, short, dense, without wave or feathering, giving fairly hard feel to the touch; weather-resistant undercoat.
coat.notes: AKC (S52): 'It should be short, straight and very dense, giving a fairly hard feeling to the hand.' RKC (S50): 'Coat length: Short'.

tail.value: 'otter' tail: very thick at base, tapering, medium length, no feathering; not curled over back
tail.quote: Distinctive feature, very thick towards base, gradually tapering towards tip, medium length, free from feathering, but clothed thickly all round with short, thick, dense coat, thus giving "rounded" appearance described as "Otter" tail. May be carried gaily, but should not curl over back.
tail.notes: Returned in four consecutive fragments; RKC (S51) identical.

ears.value: hanging, not large or heavy, close to head, set rather far back
ears.quote: Not large or heavy, hanging close to head and set rather far back.
ears.notes: RKC (S51) identical. Only one ear type → no variation in game.

eyes.value: brown or hazel (AKC: brown in black and yellow; brown or hazel in chocolate)
eyes.quote: Medium size, expressing intelligence and good temper; brown or hazel.
eyes.notes: AKC (S52): 'Eye color should be brown in black and yellow Labradors, and brown or hazel in chocolates.'

akc_traits.notes: Not reachable 2026-10-09 — see sources.md 'Looked for but not found'.

golden_retriever._note: Added 2026-10-09 (M5-R10-02). Quotes as returned by the web-fetch tool on 2026-10-09; spot-check before import (sources.md S63–S75, reused S8, S10, S11, S15, S34, S35, S54).

identity.value: FCI No. 111, Group 8 Section 1 (Retrievers), Great Britain
identity.quote: Standard number: 111; Group n°8 - Chiens rapporteurs de gibier - Chiens leveurs de gibier - Chiens d'eau; Section: Rapporteurs de gibier; Country of origin: GRANDE-BRETAGNE
identity.notes: FCI standard (S63): 'Group 8 Retrievers, Flushing Dogs, Water Dogs' / 'Section 1 Retrievers'; 'UTILIZATION: Gundog.' Definitive FCI acceptance 02/12/1954 (S64). NOTE: as for the Labrador, both S63 and S64 give 'DATE OF PUBLICATION OF THE OFFICIAL VALID STANDARD: 08.09.2026' (EN version 06.10.2026) — very recent revision; verify on fci.be.

fci_range.notes: Returned as two fragments ('Males 56 - 61 cm', 'Females 51 - 56 cm'). RKC standard (S66) identical: 'Height at withers: dogs: 56-61 cms (22-24 ins); bitches: 51-56 cms (20-22 ins).' PDSA (S68): 'Height: 51-61 cm'. Unlike the Labrador, FCI/RKC give a range, not an ideal.

rkc_range.quote: Height at withers: dogs: 56-61 cms (22-24 ins); bitches: 51-56 cms (20-22 ins).

akc_range.quote: Males 23 to 24 inches in height at withers; females 21½ to 22½ inches.
akc_range.notes: AKC range is narrower and sits in the upper half of the FCI/RKC range.

akc.unit: kg (converted from dogs 65–75 lb, bitches 55–65 lb)
akc.quote: Weight for dogs 65 to 75 pounds; bitches 55 to 65 pounds.
akc.notes: AKC standard (approved 13 Oct 1981, reformatted 18 Aug 1990). Overall 24.9–34.0 kg. FCI (S63) and RKC (S66) standards give no weight.

pdsa.notes: Key-facts box ('Average'). Woodgreen (S69): 'Weight: 25-34 kg'. Consistent with AKC.

uk_measured_mean.notes: Not found: no Golden Retriever VetCompass paper with measured bodyweight was reachable (see sources.md 'Looked for but not found').

salt_category.value: IV/V boundary (AKC 24.9–34.0 kg spans Category IV 15–<30 and V 30–<40)
salt_category.quote: Category IV: 15 to <30 kg; Category V: 30 to <40 kg
salt_category.notes: Category assignment by weight is ours (same method as the Labrador); Salt 2017 breed list not checked (PMC not reachable).

adult_weight_reached.notes: Size-class value, not breed-specific. AKC males 65–75 lb are 'Large'; bitches 55–65 lb straddle Medium (24–59 lb: 12–15 months) and Large. Salt (S8): 'larger breeds requiring up to 24 months to reach adult body weight'. Same as the Labrador.

weight_by_month_kg.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. Not derived, same reason as the Labrador: the existing logistic curve is a medium-breed curve and would contradict the large-breed 15–18 months (S10). Open question for David (shared with the Labrador).

median_uk.notes: Dogs Trust summary of McMillan et al. 2024 (S15): 'dogs with typical shaped faces e.g., Border Collie (13.1 years) or Golden Retriever (13.2 years)'. The page does not label the value 'median' (it uses 'median' only for all purebreds, 12.7 y); the Border Collie 13.1 in the same sentence equals the corrected Fig. 3 median (S16/S54), so it is very likely the median. The Golden is NOT in the corrected Fig. 3 legend (S54 checked 2026-10-09); the full paper (nature.com) was not reachable — verify the 13.2 in its supplementary table. Conflicts with S71 (12.48 y).

median_uk_vetcompass_2012.notes: O'Neill et al. VetCompass conference poster (SVEPM 2012), Table 1 row: breed, n deaths = 117, median 12.48 y, IQR 10.99–13.98. 'From a cohort of 111,293 dogs on the VetCompass database, 4,728 deaths were identified.' (92 UK practices, 2007–2011). Poster = preliminary data of the O'Neill 2013 Vet J paper (S17); small n → medium.

senior_from.notes: Derived: AAHA senior = last 25% of lifespan (S11) × 13.2 y (S15) → 0.75 × 13.2 = 9.9 y = 118.8 → 119 months. With the VetCompass median 12.48 y (S71): 0.75 × 12.48 = 9.36 y = 112 months. Dogs Trust rule of thumb > 7 y (S14).

adult.quote: Exercise: More than 2 hours per day
adult.notes: PDSA (S68) agrees: 'Your Golden Retriever will need a minimum of two hours of good exercise per day.' Woodgreen (S69) lower: 'Exercise needs: 60-90 mins'. Guide Dogs UK (S70) gives no minutes: 'Golden retrievers are active, large dogs who need daily exercise as adults.' (it advises spreading activity across the day). Two tier-B sources ≥ 2 h vs one 60–90 min → medium.

energy.quote: Golden Retrievers can be a great family dog for an active family due to their high energy levels...
energy.notes: Sentence truncated by the tool after 'levels'. FCI (S63) / RKC (S66): 'Symmetrical, balanced, active, powerful, level mover'.

temperament.value: biddable, intelligent, natural working ability; kindly, friendly and confident
temperament.quote: Characteristics: Biddable, intelligent and possessing natural working ability. Temperament: Kindly, friendly and confident.
temperament.notes: FCI (S63) same wording under 'BEHAVIOUR / TEMPERAMENT'. AKC (S67): 'Friendly, reliable, and trustworthy.' Guide Dogs (S70): 'They're also known to be calm, outgoing and sociable in nature.' Woodgreen (S69): 'a Golden is usually a calm friendly and affectionate breed.'

food_motivation.quote: Golden retrievers are known to be motivated by food and play, making them easy to train.
food_motivation.notes: Guide Dogs advises taking training treats from the daily food allowance to avoid weight gain (paraphrase of the page). No genetic study like the Labrador POMC deletion (S57) was looked up for the Golden.

obesity_tendency.quote: It’s also really important to keep your Retriever in shape, as they can easily become overweight.
obesity_tendency.notes: No prevalence figure found (no reachable Golden VetCompass paper).

mouthy_retrieving.value: mouthy as puppies (nip, play-bite); like to carry things; bred to retrieve
mouthy_retrieving.quote: As puppies, it’s normal for Retrievers to be ‘mouthy’, which means they have a tendency to nip and play bite.
mouthy_retrieving.notes: PDSA (S68): 'As their name suggests, retrieving is what they were bred for, so nearly all Golden Retrievers love a good game of fetch!' Woodgreen (S69): 'Golden Retrievers like to have things in their mouth' and 'Some Golden’s have been known to take a person's hand or wrist in their mouth and lead them around.'

chewing.quote: Like all dogs, Golden Retrievers like to chew,...
chewing.notes: Sentence truncated by the tool; PDSA frames it as normal dog behaviour, NOT a breed trait and not tied to boredom → not used for chews_when_bored. S61 (Labrador column) speaks of 'Retrievers' in general — tier C, not reused.

family.value: great family dog for an active family; can be fantastic with children (supervise)
family.quote: If you have a young family then Golden Retrievers can be fantastic with children.
family.notes: PDSA also: 'Golden Retrievers can be a great family dog for an active family…' and advises always supervising dogs with children (paraphrase). Guide Dogs (S70): 'With friendly faces and happy wagging tails, golden retrievers often make much-loved family dogs.' (also says supervise around young children). RKC gundog-group text (S65, not breed-specific): 'They make good companions, their temperament making them ideal all-round family dogs.'

time_alone.value: ≤ 4 h (generic PDSA rule for all dogs)
time_alone.quote: Remember, it’s recommended that you never leave your dog alone for more than four hours.
time_alone.notes: Generic advice, not breed-specific → no often_alone tag. Woodgreen (S69) lists 'Ability to stay home alone' without a value.

health._note: Parent-facing background only; not proposed as a game mechanic (child audience). No cancer statistic is shown anywhere in the app (David 2026-10-09).

cancer.value: high cancer risk; ~60 % estimated to die of cancer (US estimate)
cancer.quote: It is estimated that about 60 percent of Golden Retrievers die from cancer.
cancer.notes: Golden Retriever Club of America (parent club) letter on the Morris Animal Foundation Golden Retriever Lifetime Study (S73). MAF report (S72): 'Higher incidence of cancer (up to 60 percent estimated)'; 'Full Enrollment Reached in 2015 with 3,044 dogs'; 'Cancer* 28 deaths' of 69 deaths by 31 Dec 2017 (early, young cohort — not a lifetime rate). Woodgreen (S69): 'Sadly, Retrievers are also prone to a few different cancers.' The 60 % is an estimate quoted by the funder/parent club, not a peer-reviewed figure found here; PDSA (S68) does not mention cancer.

joints_eyes.value: hip and elbow dysplasia; several inherited eye conditions
joints_eyes.quote: Golden Retrievers can be prone to both hip and elbow dysplasia
joints_eyes.notes: Woodgreen (S69): 'Goldens are also at risk of a few different eye conditions that can result in blindness.' PDSA (S68) lists hip/elbow dysplasia, eye problems (cataracts, multifocal retinal dysplasia, PRA, RPED, glaucoma) and ichthyosis (list as summarised by the tool — not a verbatim quote).

coren_rank.notes: Coren's own article (S34, reachable 2026-10-09) lists the top 10 with 'Golden Retriever' as no. 4 (list item; the quote is the list entry). Wikipedia (S35): '| 4 | Golden Retriever |'. Same 'brightest' tier as the Border Collie (1) and Labrador (7). S34 also: 'Golden Retrievers earned 1,284' AKC obedience degrees in one year. Verify in the book.

coren_tier.quote: Understanding of new commands: fewer than 5 repetitions.; Obey first command: 95% of the time or better.;
coren_tier.notes: Same tier as Border Collie and Labrador (ranks 1–10). Tier definitions from Wikipedia; verify in book.

training_notes.value: thrives on training, very intelligent; easy to train
training_notes.quote: Golden Retrievers thrive off training and are very intelligent dogs.
training_notes.notes: PDSA key fact: 'Easy to train'; PDSA: 'They can be easy dogs to train and can make good first dogs for new dog owners,…'. Guide Dogs (S70): 'motivated by food and play, making them easy to train'. Woodgreen (S69): 'Training: Moderately easy' (same as the Labrador).

general.value: symmetrical, balanced, active, powerful, level mover; kindly expression
general.quote: Symmetrical, balanced, active, powerful, level mover; sound with kindly expression.

colours.quote: Any shade of gold or cream, neither red nor mahogany.
colours.notes: RKC (S66) adds: 'A few white hairs on chest only, permissible.' RKC breed page (S65) lists standard colours 'Cream, Gold, Golden'. AKC (S67): 'Rich, lustrous golden of various shades.' (AKC does not list cream). Colour frequencies: not sourced.

colour_weights.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. No source gives colour frequencies. Game could vary shade continuously from cream to dark gold, excluding red/mahogany (S63).

coat.value: flat or wavy with good feathering; dense water-resisting undercoat
coat.quote: Flat or wavy with good feathering, dense water-resisting undercoat.
coat.notes: RKC (S66) identical. AKC (S67): 'Dense and water-repellent with good undercoat.' 'Outer coat firm and resilient, neither coarse nor silky, lying close to body; may be straight or wavy.' RKC breed page (S65): 'Coat length: Medium'; PDSA (S68): 'medium to long coats'.

tail.value: level with back, reaching to hocks, no curl at tip
tail.quote: Set on and carried level with back, reaching to hocks, without curl at tip.

ears.value: moderate size, set about level with the eyes (drop ears)
ears.quote: Moderate size, set on approximate level with eyes.
ears.notes: RKC (S66) identical. Only one ear type → no variation in game.

eyes.value: dark brown, dark rims (AKC: medium brown acceptable)
eyes.quote: Dark brown, set well apart, dark rims.
eyes.notes: RKC (S66) identical. AKC (S67): 'Color preferably dark brown; medium brown acceptable.'

akc_traits.notes: Not reachable 2026-10-09 — see sources.md 'Looked for but not found'.

rkc_grooming.quote: Grooming: More than once a week
rkc_grooming.notes: Labrador: 'Once a week' (S50). PDSA (S68): 'Ideally, they should be brushed or combed three times a week at a minimum.' (daily during coat changes).

rkc_shedding.notes: PDSA (S68): 'Golden Retrievers have medium to long coats and generally do shed a lot.' Woodgreen (S69): 'Shedding: High' (Labrador: Moderate).

pdsa_children.quote: If you have a young family then Golden Retrievers can be fantastic with children.

David accepted the `children` tag on this statement (2026-10-09); the supervision caveat stays recorded here and `small_children` is not used.

pdsa_first_time_owner.quote: They can be easy dogs to train and can make good first dogs for new dog owners,...
pdsa_first_time_owner.notes: Truncated by the tool after 'owners,'. The Labrador's PDSA page had no such statement.

pdsa_time_alone.quote: Remember, it’s recommended that you never leave your dog alone for more than four hours.
pdsa_time_alone.notes: Generic for all dogs, not a breed rating.

medium_mixed_breed._note: No breed standard exists. All values below are SIZE-CLASS data (general_by_size) applied to an assumed medium size; the size assumption itself is a proposal.

assumed_adult_weight.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. Proposal: use Salt category IV (S8) as the 'medium' band. Alternative: PetMD medium 10.9–26.8 kg (S10). David to choose.

weight_by_month_kg.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. = assumed adult band × logistic %.

median_uk_crossbreeds.quote: This was slightly shorter for crossbred dogs at 12.0 years.
median_uk_crossbreeds.notes: CONFLICT: O'Neill 2013 (S17) found crossbreds lived 1.2 years LONGER than purebreds.

senior_from.notes: Derived: 0.75 × 12.0 y (S11, S15). Dogs Trust rule of thumb > 7 y (S14).
senior_from.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: senior from 108 months (0.75 × 12.0 y)

adult.quote: all adult dogs should receive between 30 minutes and two hours
adult.notes: General adult range; no mixed-breed-specific source.

adult_game_target.notes: UNSOURCED in the literature — game value inside the sourced 30–120 range (S24).

coren.quote: Non-AKC/CKC recognized breeds like Jack Russell Terriers were excluded from rankings
coren.notes: Coren ranked breeds recognised by AKC/CKC only (judges ranked breeds); mixed breeds therefore have NO rank.

breed_effect_on_behaviour.value: breed explains ~9% of individual behaviour variation
breed_effect_on_behaviour.quote: Breed explains just 9% of behavioral variation in individuals
breed_effect_on_behaviour.notes: Supports modelling a mixed breed as 'average with individual randomness'; the size of the random spread is a proposal.

game_model.value: average learning speed + individual random factor
game_model.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. REALISM_SPEC §4 idea; the numeric spread is not sourced.

learning_multiplier.notes: UNSOURCED as a number — game baseline. Mixed breeds have no Coren rank (S35); breed explains only ~9 % of individual behaviour (S42), so the mixed breed is the average dog.
learning_multiplier.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-06: the mixed breed is the baseline (1.0) (M5-R03)

individual_variation.unit: ± share of the learning speed, drawn once per dog
individual_variation.notes: UNSOURCED as a number — game value for 'average + individual randomness' (game_model). S42: breed explains ~9 % of behavioural variation, individuals vary. Uniform draw in [0.8, 1.2], seeded per pet and stored (pets.training_learning_factor).
individual_variation.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-06: mixed breed = baseline with a per-pet random factor ±20 % (M5-R03)

standard.notes: No standard exists for mixed breeds — nothing to cite for colour/ear/coat frequencies.

distribution.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. No shelter-intake statistics on mixed-breed appearance were found. Current breed_appearance.php 'mutt' options remain unsourced.

three_three_three_rule.quote: the first three days should be used for adjusting to their new surroundings, the next three weeks for training and bonding, and the first three months for continued socialization and training
three_three_three_rule.notes: Stated by a local US shelter (Longmont Humane Society) as 'a guideline'. ORIGIN UNKNOWN — no national body or study found that defines it.

adjustment_literature_range.quote: adoption literature has varyingly indicated that this process can range from four to six weeks or up to three months

adjustment_observed.quote: Over half of participants perceived the adjustment period to last longer than four months.

post_adoption_issues.notes: n=27; percentages via Faunalytics summary + paper.

c_barq_6_months.quote: Separation-related behaviors: Decrease reported at 180 days
c_barq_6_months.notes: n=99, Ohio. Prevalence = any non-zero C-BARQ score, so numbers look high; not severity.

shelter_age_distribution.quote: Puppies (≤6 months): 26% of admissions; Adults (>6 months): 74%
shelter_age_distribution.notes: Queensland RSPCA, 2014, n=11,967. Admissions, not adoptions; Australia only.

bought_puppy_age.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. REALISM_SPEC draft; consistent with training start ~8 weeks (S36) but no source on purchase age was collected.

proposed_game_parameters._note: Everything here is a PROPOSAL derived from the values above; see README for the derivation. Not facts.

feed_windows.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. From feeding_meals_per_day (S18, S21, S19, S14). Window clock times are UNSOURCED.
feed_windows.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: meal counts as listed; senior = 2

walk_minutes_puppy.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. 5 min × months × 2 (S24) — contested rule (S25).
walk_minutes_puppy.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: 10 min × age in months

step_goal_border_collie_adult.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. 120 min (S5) × 100 steps/min (S45, adult heuristic).

accident_window_hours.unit: hours a puppy can hold, by age in months
accident_window_hours.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. 1 h per month of age (S30, S31).
accident_window_hours.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-06: 1 h of hold per month of age (game rule accident_hold_hours_per_age_month = 1), puppy stage only; the clock counts only outside quiet hours and restarts at take-out, accident, birth and family-local midnight

chewing_risk.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. From S32, S33, S7.
chewing_risk.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-06: teething puppies (teething_months) chew occasionally, at most once per local day; any dog whose previous day's walk goal was missed chews once the next day

chewing_teething_chance_per_day.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal (Claude, M5-R02, waiting for David). S32 / S33 say teething puppies chew a lot but give no frequency; 0.5 = about every other day during teething_months. Stored verified = false.

training_minigame_minutes.unit: minutes of mini-game per dog and family-local day (budget)
training_minigame_minutes.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal (Claude, M5-R03, waiting for David). S36/S37: 5–10 min sessions, ≤15 min/day for puppies. Used as the dog's daily training budget (one mini-game session ≈ 50 s, so ≤ 6 sessions a day); same for every stage (no source for adults).
training_minigame_minutes.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-06: 5 minutes of mini-game per dog and day, shared equally by the children who care for the dog (M5-R03b)

feed_window_times.notes: UNSOURCED in the literature (clock times; the meal COUNT is sourced, S18). Derivation: first window 07:00, last 19:00, equal spacing, 2 h each. A window entirely inside quiet hours is done by the parent.
feed_window_times.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: 2-hour windows (was a 1-hour proposal), start times kept

arrival_age_months.notes: UNSOURCED in the literature except the puppy (~8 weeks, S36): representative age = first month of the stage, so the dog stays in that stage for the 12-week challenge.
arrival_age_months.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: puppy 2 months, other stages the first month of the stage

senior_exercise_minutes.notes: UNSOURCED in the literature: 75 % of the adult minutes. Sources only say "frequent short walks instead of one long one" (S14) and that energy needs fall with age (S13).
senior_exercise_minutes.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: senior = 75 % of the adult minutes

training_progress_per_success.unit: percentage points of command progress per correctly timed praise (mixed-breed baseline, before the breed / individual factors)
training_progress_per_success.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal (Claude, M5-R03, waiting for David). Game balance: a session has 8 cues; about 16 good daily sessions teach one command to a mixed breed (≈ 8 for a Border Collie), so all four commands take about the 12-week challenge with one session a day.
training_progress_per_success.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-06: +1 point per correctly timed praise (× breed × individual factor)

training_decay_per_missed_day.unit: percentage points lost by every command per family-local day whose training routine was missed
training_decay_per_missed_day.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal (Claude, M5-R03, waiting for David). REALISM_SPEC §4 / David 2026-10-06: without practice progress slowly decays; no source gives a rate. A day excused like the walk (hard stop / vet ≥ 50 % of the day) or the birth day never decays.
training_decay_per_missed_day.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-06: −2 points per missed training day, every command

potty_training_accident_reduction.unit: share of due puppy accidents avoided at 100 % potty training (linear in progress)
potty_training_accident_reduction.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal (Claude, M5-R03, waiting for David). A house-trained puppy learns to 'ask' to go out (S47); full house training takes 4–6 months (S31). The bladder physics (1 h per month of age, S30 / S31) stay unchanged: when the hold runs out, a trained puppy signals instead of having an accident with this probability, and its clock restarts.
potty_training_accident_reduction.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-07: a puppy at 100 % potty training avoids 3 of 4 due accidents (linear in progress); the size of the effect is PetPrep's

place_training_chewing_reduction.unit: share of the teething chewing chance removed at 100 % 'place' training (linear in progress)
place_training_chewing_reduction.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal (Claude, M5-R03, waiting for David). ASPCA: guidance teaches a puppy to restrict chewing to its toys (S33). Applies to the teething chance only — the chewing after a missed walk stays certain (David 2026-10-06).
place_training_chewing_reduction.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-07: 100 % place training halves the teething chewing chance (linear in progress); chewing after a missed walk stays certain; the size of the effect is PetPrep's

training_starting_progress.unit: training progress % per command when the dog arrives in that life stage (bought or adopted)
training_starting_progress.notes: UNSOURCED — Claude proposal (M5-R03b): a dog that arrives grown has usually learnt some basics in its previous home or shelter; no source gives numbers. Applied once at pet creation, only for pets with training; not a session.
training_starting_progress.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-06: young, adult and senior arrivals start with sit 50 %, potty 70 %, come 30 %, place 0 %; a puppy (also bought) starts at 0 %

step_goal_adult.notes: Game value (no literature step count). 90 min (Guide Dogs UK 'at least 90 minutes of exercise daily', S59) × 100 steps/min (S45, adult heuristic) — same method as the Border Collie. Alternatives recorded, not chosen: RKC 'More than 2 hours per day' (S50) → 12,000 (= Border Collie); Woodgreen 60–90 min (S60) → 6,000–9,000.
step_goal_adult.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-09: 90 min (Guide Dogs UK ≥ 90 min, S59) × 100 steps/min → 9,000 steps; keeps the Labrador apart from the Border Collie (12,000)

exercise_minutes_adult.notes: Game value = Guide Dogs UK lower bound (S59; see labrador_retriever.exercise for the exact quote). RKC (S50) says more than 2 hours, Woodgreen (S60) 60–90 min.
exercise_minutes_adult.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-09: 90 min/day (RKC '>2 h' S50 and Woodgreen 60–90 min S60 recorded as alternatives)

exercise_minutes_senior.notes: Game value (no literature number). 75 % of the adult 90 min (senior rule David confirmed for other breeds 2026-10-05) = 67.5 min; minutes are whole numbers (StageParamKey::validate, API exercise_minutes int) → 68 min = 6,800 steps.
exercise_minutes_senior.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-09: 68 min → 6,800 steps (75 % of 90 = 67.5, rounded to whole minutes)

stage_boundaries_months.notes: Game boundaries (no exact month in the literature). young 9: AAHA 'cessation of rapid growth (~6–9 months, varying with breed and size)' (S11) — same as the other dogs. Large-breed evidence: growth ends 15–18 months (S10 'Large (59–99 pounds): 15–18 months'), up to 24 months (S8); AAHA's young-adult boundary is cessation of RAPID growth, not end of growth, so 9 months still fits (alternative 12 not chosen). adult 36: AAHA 3–4 years (S11), same as other breeds. senior 118 = 0.75 × 13.1 y (S11 + S54); 108 if the VetCompass median 12.0 y (S55) were used (not chosen).
stage_boundaries_months.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-09: young 9, adult 36, senior 118 (0.75 × McMillan 2024 median 13.1 y, S54)

arrival_age_months.notes: Game value (no literature number). First month of each stage (rule David confirmed 2026-10-05), so the dog stays in its stage for the 12-week challenge.
arrival_age_months.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-09: first month of each stage (2 / 9 / 36 / 118)

learning_multiplier.notes: Game value (no literature factor). Coren rank 7 is in the same 'brightest' tier as the Border Collie (<5 repetitions, ≥95 % first-command obedience; S35, tier C); the tier is Coren's only quantitative statement, so the evidence alone would give 2.0 — David chose 1.8 so the Border Collie stays visibly fastest. No individual variation (like the Border Collie; S42 says breed explains only ~9 % of individual behaviour — not used). Food motivation (S59, S57) could later justify a treat-training bonus.
learning_multiplier.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-09: 1.8 — same Coren 'brightest' tier as the Border Collie (2.0), BC stays visibly fastest

step_goal_adult.notes: Game value (no literature step count). 120 min (RKC 'More than 2 hours per day', S65; PDSA 'a minimum of two hours of good exercise per day', S68) × 100 steps/min (S45, adult heuristic) — same method as the Border Collie / Labrador. Unlike the Labrador (PDSA gave no minutes, Guide Dogs gave ≥ 90), two tier-B sources agree on ≥ 2 h and Guide Dogs (S70) gives no number. Alternatives recorded, not chosen: 90 min → 9,000 (= Labrador; Woodgreen upper bound S69); Woodgreen 60–90 min → 6,000–9,000.
step_goal_adult.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-09: 120 min (RKC S65 '> 2 h' + PDSA S68 'minimum of two hours') × 100 steps/min → 12,000 steps (= Border Collie)

exercise_minutes_adult.notes: Game value = PDSA 'minimum of two hours' (S68) = RKC '> 2 h' (S65) lower bound. Woodgreen 60–90 min (S69) recorded as alternative (90), not chosen.
exercise_minutes_adult.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-09: 120 min/day (Woodgreen 60–90 min S69 recorded as alternative)

exercise_minutes_senior.notes: Game value (no literature number). 75 % of the adult 120 min (senior rule David confirmed 2026-10-05) = 90 min exactly → 9,000 steps (= Border Collie senior).

stage_boundaries_months.notes: Game boundaries (no exact month in the literature). young 9 / adult 36: AAHA (S11), same reasoning as the Labrador (large-breed growth ends 15–18 months, S10, but AAHA's young-adult boundary is cessation of RAPID growth; alternative young 12 not chosen). senior 119 = 0.75 × 13.2 y × 12 = 118.8 → 119 (S11 + S15, Dogs Trust summary of McMillan 2024). Alternatives not chosen: 112 = 0.75 × 12.48 y (VetCompass poster, S71); 118 (= Labrador / Border Collie). 119 is 1 month later than the Labrador / Border Collie (118).
stage_boundaries_months.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-09: young 9, adult 36, senior 119 (0.75 × 13.2 y, S15 Dogs Trust summary of McMillan 2024)

learning_multiplier.notes: Game value (no literature factor). Coren rank 4 (S34, S35) — same 'brightest' tier as the Border Collie (rank 1 → 2.0) and the Labrador (rank 7 → 1.8). Linear between them by rank: 2.0 − (4−1)/(7−1) × 0.2 = 1.9 → keeps the Border Collie fastest and the order of Coren's list. PDSA 'Easy to train' (S68), Guide Dogs 'motivated by food and play, making them easy to train' (S70); Woodgreen 'Moderately easy' (S69, same as the Labrador). No individual variation (like the Border Collie and the Labrador). Alternatives not chosen: 1.8 (= Labrador), 2.0 (= tier only).
learning_multiplier.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-09: 1.9 (Coren rank 4, S34) — between the Border Collie (2.0) and the Labrador (1.8)

grooming_mechanic.notes: UNSOURCED idea, not built (post-MVP backlog; no decision asked).
